## My Reasoning

I've been farming this land in Quzhou for over 40 years. My fields sit on the North China Plain — flat, loamy soil, reliable enough in summer rain but bone-dry the rest of the year. The groundwater here has been dropping for decades; I've watched the pump depth on my well go from 20 meters to nearly 60. That shapes everything I do.

At my age and with the knowledge I've built up, I don't experiment recklessly. The wheat-maize rotation is what this land is for, what my neighbors do, what the market expects, and what I know how to do well. I'll grow winter wheat on my 10 mu, then follow immediately with summer maize on the same land. Two crops, one year, same plot — that's the Quzhou way.

I'll use an improved wheat variety — probably Jimai 22 or Kenong 199, both well-tested here for yield and drought tolerance. For maize I'll use a hybrid like Xianyu 335; the yield advantage over open-pollinated seed is too large to ignore and I can afford the seed cost.

On fertilizer, I've learned from the university extension work done in this county. Many farmers overapply nitrogen — I used to as well. Now I apply closer to the agronomic optimum: enough to feed the crop, not the groundwater. I split my wheat nitrogen: base application at seeding, topdress at jointing.

Water is my biggest constraint. I will irrigate wheat twice — at jointing and heading — no more. The research from Quzhou consistently shows a third irrigation rarely pays back in yield what it costs in water and electricity. For summer maize, the monsoon usually covers it; I'll irrigate once at emergence if June is dry, otherwise I'll let the rain do the work.

For tillage, I rotary-till before wheat seeding to incorporate the maize straw. After wheat harvest I direct-seed the maize into the stubble — saves fuel, saves time, and at 65 I'm happy to save my back.
